newsitem.title: KENYA: Foreign investors quit Kenya after IMF ruling.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors quit Kenya after IMF ruling.

text.p: Foreign investors pulled out of the Nairobi Stock Exchange in droves on Friday after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) announced the cancellation of a big aid package to Kenya, bourse officials said.

Foreign investors sold 250 million shillings ($4.1 million) of the fourth issue of the Central Bank of Kenya floating-rate treasury bond on Friday compared with a sale of only 13.35 million shillings during the whole of last week, they said.
Some 800,000 shillings in corporate bonds of the East African Development Bank were sold by foreign investors as they joined in a stampede to leave the country.
The Nairobi Stock Exchange 20-share index lost 13.68 points to stand at 3453.18. But turnover increased to 26.6 million from 20.1 million reflecting high volumes changing hands.

"Most of the investors are treading blindly, they're waiting for the dust to settle after the IMF announcement," said one broker. Another said the foreign boards were quiet, as worried investors adopted a policy of wait and see.
"Now that we've lost the IMF package, many foreign investors are suspending their orders or making cancellations," said a senior trader.

He added that since overseas investors account for up to 40 percent of bourse business, and on good days up to 50 percent, their loss of confidence would deal a severe blow to this leading east African emerging market.
"If foreigners start selling that could crush the market," he said.
Anxious brokers called for President Daniel arap Moi's discredited government to send clear signals that it was still committed to economic reforms and liberalisation.
"Unless the government acts very fast the effect (of the IMF cancellation) is going to be devastating," said a bourse official.

Turnover was pushed up by activity on the agricultural board, as brokers predicted increasing profits from dollar-earning exporters as the Kenya shilling slumped to rates as low as 64.50 to the dollar, compared to around 59 at the close of trade on Thursday.
The IMF halted its lending programme to Kenya on Thursday amid mounting concern that the government was not doing enough to crack down on corruption.

The Fund said a $205 million three-year loan, offered under the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, would be allowed to lapse because the government's response to a July 24 deadline had been inadequate.
